what_it_does: Safety-critical embedded computers — think a self-driving car's control unit or a robot's brain — run the Linux operating system kernel (the software layer that controls all hardware resources). An attacker who tampers with the kernel's code or data in memory can take over the device completely, so security teams want continuous checks that kernel memory has not been altered. The standard approach is to periodically compute a fingerprint (a cryptographic hash — a mathematical summary) of key kernel data and compare it to a known-good value, but doing this thoroughly enough to catch attacks uses too much processor time on small embedded chips. LightRIM cuts that cost with two ideas: first, it hashes kernel objects in two stages, only recomputing the outer fingerprint when an inner sub-fingerprint flags a change, so most checks are very cheap. Second, instead of checking everything on a fixed clock schedule (which a clever attacker could exploit by making changes between checks), the system randomizes when it measures each object — this closes the window where an attacker could temporarily alter data and restore it before the next check (a timing attack known as a TOCTOU, or 'time-of-check to time-of-use' vulnerability). A heuristic algorithm decides which objects to check and how often, maximizing the chance of catching an attack while staying within the CPU budget.
